title: Decryption failures as approximate DDGR hints: measured block-size drop per observed failure on reduced ML-KEM
claim: Each decryption failure observed for an attacker-generated ML-KEM ciphertext conditions the secret (s,e) to satisfy |<(s,e),c> + known| > q/4 along a public direction c built from (r,e1,e2). Integrated as approximate hints (truncated-Gaussian posterior along c) in the DDGR distorted-BDD framework, F failures lower the measured success block size of progressive BKZ on reduced instances by at least 2 per failure over the first 4 failures, and the DDGR leaky-LWE estimator predicts the measured success beta within +-3. If the measured drop is within the A/A noise floor, or the estimator misses by more than 5, the claim is false.
mechanism: Failure-boosting literature (D'Anvers et al.) uses failures to estimate a secret direction and then argues a lattice gain informally. DDGR shows any linear hint with a known posterior can be folded into the BDD ellipsoid, shrinking the volume along c. A failure is a one-sided inequality on a projection, whose posterior has variance reduced and mean shifted away from 0; the variance reduction along c is the information gained. Because the conditioning is along F nearly independent directions, the lattice dimension effectively loses roughly a fraction of a dimension per failure. Measuring this directly closes the gap between the failure-oracle cost (query count) and the lattice cost that follows.
tracked_object: Success block size beta* (smallest progressive-BKZ/G6K pump block size at which the planted secret is recovered and verified) on the hint-integrated DBDD instance, as a function of the number F of integrated failures.

title: Rotation-augmented sieve database on negacyclic module lattices: does the 2n-fold rotation orbit survive projection into BKZ blocks?
claim: On the full (unprojected) primal lattice of a module-LWE instance over Z[X]/(X^n+1), inserting all 2n signed rotations of each new short vector into a G6K database cuts the number of sieve iterations to saturation by a factor >= 4 at lattice dimension 64-96. Inside BKZ the projected block pi_i(L) is not rotation invariant, so the gain must collapse to <= 1.1x once the block is a proper projection. The falsifiable content is the collapse curve as a function of projection depth.
mechanism: The module lattice is invariant under multiplication by X acting coordinatewise on each ring component, so each lattice vector carries an orbit of 2n vectors of equal norm (Schneider; Bos-Naehrig-van de Pol exploited this for ideal Gauss sieving). Projection orthogonal to the first i Gram-Schmidt vectors destroys the invariance because the projection subspace is not X-stable. The fraction of the orbit that stays short after projection decays with i. Measuring that decay tells whether any rotation saving can reach the projected sieves that dominate the real attack.
tracked_object: Ratio of sieve iterations (and total pair tests) to reach 90% saturation, rotation-augmented vs plain, as a function of projection depth i into the lattice.

predictions.metric: iteration ratio plain/augmented at i=0 (full lattice)

predictions.falsified_by: ratio >= 1.5 at i=d/4, which would mean rotation structure survives projection

minimal_test.design: Primal embedding lattices of module-LWE with n in {16,32}, k in {2,3} (d=64..96). For each, run G6K sieve on context [i, d] for i in {0, 4, 8, d/8, d/4, d/2} with and without inserting rotated copies (projected) of every newly found vector; count iterations, pair tests and wall time to saturation.
controls: null: unstructured q-ary lattice of the same dimension and determinant with 'rotations' applied as random signed coordinate permutations (orbit is not in the lattice) - augmentation must not help
positive: ideal lattice (k=1) full sieve, where the orbit is exact and the published gain should reproduce
A/A: plain arm run twice with different database-initialization seed blocks

falsification_conditions: no gain at i=0 on the positive control (implementation broken)
P2 violated: gain persists at deep projection
confounders: inserting rotations inflates the database and saturation definition
LLL preprocessing quality differs by instance
thread scheduling noise in G6K
interpretation_limits: At FIPS 203 dimensions the final sieve runs at i ~ d - beta >> d/4, so only a negative P2 can matter there; a positive P1 alone is a toy-dimension statement
d <= 96 only

title: Module-BKZ versus scalar BKZ in total counted operations at equal output profile, rank 2-3 modules over degree 8-32 cyclotomics
claim: At module rank 2 and 3 over Z[X]/(X^d+1), d in {8,16,32}, module-BKZ (module-LLL plus module-SVP oracles) reaches the same measured log-profile slope as scalar BKZ at a total counted cost (SVP-oracle node or sieve pair counts plus size-reduction ring multiplications) that is either at least 2x lower (structure is a liability) or at least 2x higher (structure is a cost to the attacker). The claim is that the sign is determinable at these sizes with 20 instances per cell and is not inside the A/A noise.
mechanism: IDEA-20260829-353361 measures the blocksize offset Delta(d,r) at equal slope. A blocksize offset does not by itself fix cost: module-BKZ operates on d-times smaller matrices over the ring (fast NTT multiplication), uses fewer but larger SVP calls, and the module-SVP oracle can exploit the ring automorphisms inside the block. Those terms can offset a positive Delta, or compound it. Only a total-cost measurement at matched output decides which.
tracked_object: Total counted cost (enumeration nodes or sieve pair tests, plus ring/integer multiplications in size reduction) to reach target root-Hermite slope, module-BKZ divided by scalar BKZ.

Run scalar progressive BKZ (fpylll) and module-BKZ (a SageMath prototype per Lee-Pellet-Mary-Stehle-Wallet module-LLL with enumeration-based module-SVP) until the measured profile slope reaches the same target; count operations.

title: Meet-LWE with CBD-shaped representations: do eta-ary representation weights beat the ternary analysis for CBD(2)/CBD(3) secrets at n=32-64?
claim: May's Meet-LWE representation technique, generalized to secrets with the exact CBD(eta) symbol distribution on {-eta..eta} (representations split each symbol into two summands drawn from a tuned distribution), achieves a measured time exponent c (log2 time / n) at least 10% below the same algorithm using a ternary-style representation on CBD(2) secrets at n in {32,48,64}, q=3329. It remains far above the primal lattice attack at the same n; the claim concerns the combinatorial exponent, not a break.
mechanism: Representation counts grow with the number of ways to write a symbol as a sum; CBD(eta) puts mass 6/16, 4/16, 1/16 on 0, +-1, +-2 (eta=2), so tuned summand distributions can produce more representations per list element than a ternary-weight split. More representations allow stronger filtering modulo partial q-ary constraints, shrinking lists. This changes the exponent coefficient of the combinatorial attack, which is the term hybrid attacks combine with lattice reduction.

title: Compression-error-aware failure boosting: include the attacker-known Compress_dv/Compress_du rounding errors in the weak-ciphertext score
claim: An attacker who generates ciphertexts knows the exact rounding errors introduced by Compress_du(u) and Compress_dv(v). Scoring candidate encapsulations by the full known part of the failure term, including these rounding errors, rather than by ||(r,e1)|| alone, raises the failure probability of the top 2^-10 filtered fraction by a factor >= 2 at equal precomputation, measured on reduced parameters with elevated base DFR. If the ratio is within the A/A noise, the compression terms add nothing to boosting.
mechanism: The decryption noise is e^T r - s^T(e1 + du_err) + e2 + dv_err. The attacker knows r, e1, e2, du_err and dv_err exactly; only s and e are secret. dv_err enters additively with magnitude up to q/2^(dv+1) (about 104 at dv=4), a known shift toward the failure threshold, while du_err enlarges the effective vector multiplying s. Published boosting weights only by the norms of (r,e1); conditioning on the known additive shift dv_err in the coordinate where the failure is tested changes the per-coordinate tail probability directly.
tracked_object: Empirical failure probability of the filtered ciphertext set (top fraction 2^-10 by score) under the full-known-term score vs the (r,e1)-norm score.

predictions.metric: failure rate ratio full_score / norm_score at filter 2^-10

title: Multi-key failure precomputation is killed by FIPS 203's H(ek) in G: measure the amortization factor with and without key binding
claim: In FIPS 203, (K, r) = G(m || H(ek)), so the encryption randomness of a ciphertext depends on the target public key and weak-ciphertext precomputation cannot be shared across keys. title: Learned pump-and-jump scheduling for Kyber-shaped primal instances versus G6K default and two-step-mode schedules
claim: A policy that picks the next (block size, jump, extra dimensions-for-free) from features of the current Gram-Schmidt log-profile, trained on self-generated Kyber-shaped instances at lattice dimension 140-180, reduces median counted cost to recover the secret by >= 15% versus G6K's lwe_challenge default schedule on held-out instances, and by >= 5% versus the schedule optimized by the two-step-mode estimator. Below those margins the claim is false.
mechanism: Fixed schedules assume the profile follows a GSA-like simulator after each tour. Real profiles deviate (head concavity, tail flattening) and the deviation predicts when a larger jump or an earlier final pump pays. A learned policy conditions on the observed deviation instead of a simulator, so it can skip tours that the simulator says are needed but the instance does not. The gain is a constant, but it applies directly to the end-to-end S of the current baseline.

Train a gradient-boosted policy by imitation of the best schedule found by search on training instances. Evaluate all schedules on held-out instances with paired seeds.

positive: an oracle schedule with knowledge of the planted secret's projected norm per position (upper bound on achievable gain)

title: Empirical success model for pruned enumeration in BKZ blocks: the block's shortest vector is not uniform on the sphere
claim: Inside BKZ tours on Kyber-shaped q-ary lattices, the projected coordinates of the block's shortest vector are not distributed as a uniform point on the sphere that the GNR pruning optimizer assumes; an empirical success model fitted on observed shortest vectors yields pruning coefficients that cut enumeration nodes per successful SVP call by >= 20% at block size 50-64 at equal success probability. If the empirical distribution passes a uniformity test or the node saving is < 5%, the claim is false.
mechanism: Extreme pruning computes success probability as the volume of a cylinder intersection under a uniform-direction assumption. In BKZ the block basis is already reduced, and the found vector's last coordinates are systematically smaller (it is short in the projected tail because the head is concave). If the true target concentrates, the optimal pruning profile tightens where mass is absent, saving nodes. The model is fitted on one set of tours and tested on fresh ones.

title: Noisy NTT-domain hints as extra MLWE samples: the hint-noise threshold below which they lower beta (simulated, defensive)
claim: A simulated side channel that yields noisy estimates of NTT-domain secret coefficients, s_hat_i + noise mod q with noise std sigma_h, is equivalent to T extra LWE samples on s with public vectors given by NTT rows. Integrating them in the primal embedding lowers the success block size only when sigma_h is below a threshold sigma* that we predict lies between 2 and 20 at n=64,k=2; above sigma* the drop is within A/A noise. The measured threshold and slope are the defensive deliverable: how accurate an NTT-output leakage must be before it matters to a lattice attacker.
mechanism: NTT outputs are q-ary linear combinations of all secret coefficients, so a noisy reading is a modular approximate hint that DDGR's framework (which takes approximate hints over Z or exact modular hints) does not directly handle. Rewriting the reading as an LWE sample with error sigma_h makes it integrable: it is a new row in the q-ary embedding with error column scaled by sigma_h/sigma_e. Primal gain depends on the ratio sigma_h/sigma_e and on how many such rows are added, giving a sharp threshold.
tracked_object: Measured success block size beta* versus (number of hinted NTT slots T, hint noise sigma_h), and the fitted threshold sigma*.

title: Implicit rejection leaves only a noisy key-confirmation oracle: a channel-capacity bound on failure-attack query cost, checked by simulation
claim: Under FIPS 203 implicit rejection, a decryption failure is visible to a remote attacker only as a protocol-level key mismatch, which is confounded by benign errors at rate epsilon. When epsilon exceeds the per-query failure probability p, the number of queries to collect F true failures grows by a factor at least (1 + epsilon/p) times the repetitions needed to confirm each candidate. Simulation at elevated-DFR parameters with epsilon in {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2} matches the bound within a factor 2. Defensive: it prices the oracle realism that 7c1ae4's conjunction leaves unpriced.
mechanism: Decapsulation is deterministic, so a candidate failure can be retested; benign errors are independent across retries. Confirmation then requires about log(1/delta)/log(1/epsilon) retries per alarm, and alarms arrive at rate p + epsilon. The binary asymmetric channel with crossover epsilon has capacity that bounds the information per query about the failure set. Comparing simulated query counts with the bound checks whether the confirmation strategy is near-optimal.
tracked_object: Queries per confirmed true failure versus benign-error rate epsilon at fixed filtered-ciphertext failure probability p.

predictions.metric: queries per true failure at epsilon=1e-2, p=2^-14

title: Known-plaintext ciphertexts as extra, much noisier MLWE samples on s: measure that they do not lower primal beta (control)
claim: For a known (m, ciphertext) pair, v - Decompress(m) = s^T u + noise, so each ciphertext yields n extra MLWE-like samples on s with noise std around 40 (from e^T r, s^T e1, e2 and d_v rounding) against sigma ~1 for the public key. Adding up to 16 such ciphertexts to the primal embedding lowers measured beta* by < 1 at n=64, k=2. A drop >= 3 would falsify the claim and reveal an unpriced known-plaintext flank.
mechanism: A primal attack benefits from extra samples only if their noise-to-modulus ratio is comparable to existing samples. Ciphertext-derived samples have noise roughly 40x larger, so their rows add volume nearly as fast as they add constraint; the optimal embedding should ignore them. This is a falsifiable sanity bound that every key-recovery-from-traffic claim should cite.

title: Non-oracle overhead at real FIPS 203 dimension: measured LLL, size-reduction and GSO-precision cost on full ML-KEM primal bases
claim: Core-SVP charges only the SVP oracle and treats basis maintenance (LLL, size reduction, Gram-Schmidt updates, insertion) as polynomial and free. On full primal embedding bases at the real ML-KEM-512 and ML-KEM-768 shapes (lattice dimension about 1000 to 1500, q=3329), the measured cost of the non-oracle work for one BKZ tour at small block size, with the floating-point precision the run needs to stay numerically sound, is at least 2^40 bit operations. That puts a measured floor under the polynomial factor. If it is below 2^30, the polynomial factor is negligible against any oracle cost and the convention is confirmed for this term.
mechanism: fpylll and G6K keep Gram-Schmidt data in floating point. At dimensions above about 600, double precision fails for q-ary bases with large log-profile slopes, which forces long-double, dd, qd or MPFR, and each step up multiplies the cost of every size reduction. A BKZ tour does O(d) insertions, each followed by an O(d^2) update, so per-tour maintenance is O(d^3) multiplications at the required precision. This is the one part of the attack that can be measured at the true FIPS dimension, because it needs no large SVP oracle. Core-SVP sets it to zero.
tracked_object: Counted floating-point operations, times the cost of the precision type, for LLL plus one BKZ-20 tour on full ML-KEM-shaped primal bases. Also the minimum precision type at which the run completes without a GSO-consistency failure.

title: Parallel efficiency of G6K sieving from 1 to 64 threads at d=70-85: is core-SVP time a sequential fiction under shared bandwidth?
claim: Core-SVP prices total operations as if they parallelize freely. Measured G6K throughput (pair tests per second) at d=70-85 on one node scales with efficiency E(t) = speedup/t that falls below 0.6 at t=64, and the fall steepens with d (memory-bandwidth saturation). If E(64) >= 0.85 at all d, parallel memory contention is negligible at this scale and the objection is falsified.
mechanism: Bucketed sieves share one database; as threads grow, DRAM bandwidth and cache coherence become the bottleneck rather than arithmetic. An attacker's area-time cost then includes idle arithmetic, so a parallel attack's real cost exceeds the operation count by 1/E. title: Inside one SVP call: measured progressive-sieving overhead C_prog = pump cost / final sieve cost at d=60-90 vs the geometric series
claim: Core-SVP charges one sieve at the final dimension. A G6K pump sieves progressively from small to full dimension and adds dimensions-for-free; the measured ratio C_prog of total pair tests to the final sieve's pair tests is in [3, 8] at d=60-90 and drifts by less than 1 bit across the range. The geometric-series prediction 1/(1-2^{-c}) with the measured per-dimension exponent c predicts C_prog within 1.5x. A drift > 1 bit or a miss > 2x falsifies the constant-overhead assumption.
mechanism: Progressive sieving pays a sum over dimensions of per-dimension sieve costs; if each costs 2^{c d'}, the sum is a geometric series dominated by the last term, so the overhead is a constant determined by c. But the realized c at small d (often near 0.35 not 0.292) and the extra cost of insertion and re-saturation may make the overhead grow or shrink. IDEA-20260821-41cd67 concerns the number of oracle calls R across BKZ; this is the cost inside one call.
tracked_object: C_prog per pump, and the fitted per-dimension exponent c, at sieve dimension 60-90.

minimal_test.design: G6K pumps (down_sieve off, f in {0, d4f default}) on q-ary lattices d in {60,65,...,90}, 5 instances; count pair tests per progressive step; separately run a cold final-dimension sieve for the denominator.
controls: null: a pump with step size equal to full dimension (no progression) must give C_prog ~ 1
positive: progressive step 1 vs step 4 where the series prediction changes in a computable direction
A/A: default pump with two database seed blocks

confounders: cold sieve start-up cost in denominator
saturation targets differ between pump steps and cold sieve

title: Batch-CVP after one sieve: measured per-query cost of Voronoi-slicer CVPP at d=50-70 versus the per-guess Babai cost hybrids assume
claim: Hybrid attacks pay one CVP (or BDD) per combinatorial guess, usually priced as Babai nearest-plane on a reduced basis. Using a sieve-preprocessed list for CVPP (Doulgerakis-Laarhoven-de Weger style iterative slicing), the measured per-query cost at d=50-70 for BDD targets at the hybrid's distance is 2^{c_q d} with c_q <= 0.1 and success >= 0.9 where Babai succeeds < 0.5. This changes the hybrid optimum when ported to estimator parameters by >= 3 bits. If c_q >= 0.2 or success does not exceed Babai's, the estimator's Babai pricing stands.
mechanism: With a list of short lattice vectors from one sieve, iterative slicing reduces a target toward the Voronoi cell; amortized over many targets, the per-query cost is subexponential-ish in the list size and can succeed at distances where Babai fails, allowing smaller preprocessing beta in the hybrid. Estimators fix the BDD step as Babai; the tradeoff curve between preprocessing and per-query success is unmeasured at Kyber shape.
tracked_object: Per-query counted cost and success rate of slicer CVPP vs Babai for BDD targets at relative distance r in {0.5,0.7,0.9} of the gh, on Kyber-shaped projected sublattices.

title: Does the Gaussian surrogate for CBD errors misprice primal success? Matched-variance CBD vs discrete Gaussian vs uniform beta*
claim: Estimators replace ML-KEM's CBD(eta) secret and error by Gaussians of equal variance. On primal instances at lattice dimension 120-160, the median success block size for CBD(2) differs from the matched-variance discrete Gaussian by < 1 block size, while uniform {-2..2} of different kurtosis but matched variance also differs by < 1. If any pair differs by >= 2 with CI excluding 0, the variance-only surrogate is not adequate and estimator inputs must carry the shape.
mechanism: uSVP success depends on the norm of the projected planted vector, which by concentration depends mostly on the variance; higher moments enter through the spread of the projected norm (excess kurtosis of CBD(2) is -0.25). The effect on the median beta should be small but on the spread could be visible. IDEA-20260808-90632c addresses the projected-norm ratio law; this measures the attack outcome directly.
tracked_object: Distribution of beta* for three error laws with identical variance, paired instances (same A).

minimal_test.design: Same public matrices A (n=40,k=2,q=3329), 150 instances; for each draw s,e from CBD(2), discrete Gaussian sigma=1, and uniform with variance matched by scaling support/probabilities; progressive G6K to verified recovery.
controls: null: two independent CBD(2) draws on the same A (difference must be ~0)
positive: Gaussian with variance 1.5x (beta* must increase measurably)
A/A: CBD arm with two reduction seed blocks

falsification_conditions: positive control shows no increase (instrument too coarse)
confounders: matching variance for uniform requires non-integer support weights
progressive step granularity
